1 --- 2 title: instant 3 description: API reference for the instant route segment config. 4 related: 5 title: Next Steps 6 description: Learn how to use instant navigations in practice. 7 links: 8 - app/guides/instant-navigation 9 - app/getting-started/caching 10 - app/getting-started/revalidating 11 - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache 12 --- 13 14 The `instant` route segment config controls how Next.js validates whether a navigation into this segment would produce an instant UI. 15 16 Next.js uses prefetching to preload navigations for all in-app links on the current page. However, client-side data fetching or partially prerendered results from the server can lead to navigations that don't update the UI immediately. To help you build fast-feeling navigations, `instant` lets you tell Next.js what to expect from navigations through the configured segment. For instance, you can indicate that navigations into this segment should produce a UI that renders instantly without waiting on any externally loaded data. You can also indicate that navigations aren't expected to be instant. 17 18 When a segment is configured to expect an instant UI, Next.js surfaces any code in your application that would block the navigation from updating the UI immediately. See the [Instant Navigation guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) for an end-to-end walkthrough. 19 20 > **Good to know**: 21 > 22 > - The `instant` export only works when [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) is enabled. 23 > - `instant` cannot be used in Client Components. It will throw an error. 24 > - Next.js does not perform prefetches in development, so navigations may not feel as instant as they will in production. Validation reflects what will happen during `next start`, where prefetching is enabled. 25 26 ```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx" switcher 27 export const instant = true 28 29 export default function Page() { 30 return
...
31 } 32 ``` 33 34 ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js" switcher 35 export const instant = true 36 37 export default function Page() { 38 return
...
39 } 40 ``` 41 42 ## Reference 43 44 The export accepts: 45 46 - **`true`**: Opts the segment into validation at whatever level is configured globally (see [Configuring validation defaults](#configuring-validation-defaults)). With the framework defaults, validation runs in development only and surfaces errors in the dev overlay. 47 - **`false`**: Opts the segment out (see [Disabling instant](#disabling-instant)). 48 - An **object**: Opts in with additional options. See [`level`](#level). 49 50 ### `level` 51 52 Sets the severity at which validation runs for this segment. 53 54 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 55 export const instant = { 56 level: 'warning', 57 } 58 ``` 59 60 - **`'warning'`**: Validates in development only. Errors appear in the dev overlay; the build is unaffected. 61 62 In the future a validation level that supports validation during build will be supported. Unless you are enabling experimental validation modes there is no need to specify level since the only level available is `"warning"`. 63 64 When `level` is omitted (or `instant = true` is used), the segment is validated at whatever level is configured globally — see [Configuring validation defaults](#configuring-validation-defaults). 65 66 ### Disabling instant 67 68 Set `false` on a layout or page to indicate that this segment is allowed to block when navigating to it. 69 70 This is useful when a deeper page should be instant but an ancestor can't be. For instance, if a shared layout cannot load instantly but you still want to assert that pages beneath this layout can be navigated to instantly, you can ensure that the pages have `instant = true` while the shared layout has `instant = false`. 71 72 ```tsx filename="app/tabs/layout.tsx" 73 export const instant = false 74 ``` 75 76 ```tsx filename="app/tabs/[tab]/page.tsx" 77 export const instant = true 78 ``` 79 80 Navigations from outside into a tab are allowed to block at the layout. Navigations between tabs are validated for instant UI. 81 82 You don't need to add `false` to ancestors of an instant page just because they do something blocking — a higher-up `instant = true` doesn't force its descendants to validate, and leaving an ancestor unconfigured is fine. Reach for `false` only when you've configured a deeper page as instant and need to exempt navigations that pass through a blocking ancestor. 83 84 ### Disabling static shell validation 85 86 Cache Components also validates that each page in your app produces a non-empty static shell at prerender time. To opt a route out of this validation, ensure the highest `instant` config in the route's tree is `false` — a `false` higher in the tree takes precedence over any deeper `true` for the static-shell check. 87 88 Setting `false` on the root layout disables static shell validation for the entire app. Place the `false` as low as possible — only as high as needed to cover the routes you want to opt out — so the rest of the app keeps validating. 89 90 ## How validation works 91 92 `instant` triggers validation at every shared layout boundary in the route. Validation runs during development (on page loads and HMR updates) and surfaces errors in the dev error overlay. 93 94 Each error identifies the component that would block navigation. The fix is usually to cache the data with `use cache` or wrap it in a `` boundary. 95 96 ## Configuring validation defaults 97 98 By default (`validationLevel: 'warning'`), Cache Components apps validate every Page and Default segment in development. The `experimental.instantInsights.validationLevel` config tunes this behavior — for example, to limit validation to segments that opt in explicitly via `instant`. 99 100 ```js filename="next.config.js" 101 module.exports = { 102 experimental: { 103 instantInsights: { 104 validationLevel: 'warning', 105 }, 106 }, 107 } 108 ``` 109 110 The supported levels are: 111 112 - **`'warning'`** _(framework default)_: Every Page and Default segment is implicitly validated at warning level (dev only). 113 - **`'manual-warning'`**: Only segments with an explicit `instant` are validated, at warning level (dev only). 114 115 Setting `instant = false` on a segment opts it out of validation entirely. 116 117 > **Good to know**: 118 > 119 > - The framework default may change in future versions to opt users into higher levels of validation. Because this feature is experimental, that change is not considered a breaking change. To pin a specific behavior, set `validationLevel` explicitly. 120 > - Framework-synthesized error routes (`/_global-error`, `/_not-found`) are excluded from implicit validation. To validate them, opt in explicitly with `instant`. 121 122 ## Inspecting loading states 123 124 The Navigation Inspector is available when Cache Components is enabled: 125 126 ```js filename="next.config.js" 127 module.exports = { 128 cacheComponents: true, 129 } 130 ``` 131 132 Open the Next.js DevTools and select **Navigation Inspector**, then turn on **Pause on navigations**. While the toggle is on: 133 134 - Refresh the page to freeze the initial static UI generated for the route, before any dynamic data streams in. 135 - Click a link to freeze the prefetched UI for the destination route. 136 137 When the UI is frozen, click **Resume** to let the current navigation finish. The toggle stays on, so the next refresh or link click pauses too. Turn it off when you are done. Use both page refreshes and link clicks to check that your loading states look right on first visit and on navigation. 138 139 ## Testing instant navigation 140 141 The `@next/playwright` package exports an `instant()` helper that holds back dynamic content while the callback runs against the instant UI. See the [guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation#prevent-regressions-with-e2e-tests) for a full example. 142 143 ```typescript 144 import { instant } from '@next/playwright' 145 ``` 146 147 {/* TODO: remove when fixed and from prod-docs-release */} 148 149 ## Known issue: shared cookie across projects 150 151 The DevTools use a `next-instant-navigation-testing` cookie to hold back dynamic content and freeze the page at the instant UI. Because cookies are scoped to the domain and not the port, running multiple projects on the same domain (typically `localhost`) means the cookie is shared across them and can cause unexpected behavior. Clear the cookie or close the Navigation Inspector panel when switching between projects to avoid issues. 152 153 > **Good to know:** This will be fixed as part of stabilizing the feature. 154 155 ## TypeScript 156 157 ```tsx 158 type InstantConfig = 159 | true 160 | false 161 | { 162 level?: 'warning' 163 } 164 165 export const instant: InstantConfig = true 166 ``` 167 168 ## Version History 169 170 | Version | Changes | 171 | --------- | --------------------------------------------------- | 172 | `v16.x.x` | `instant` export introduced (Cache Components only) | 173

content.content: 1 --- 2 title: Streaming 3 nav_title: Streaming 4 description: Learn how streaming works in Next.js and how to use it to progressively render UI as data becomes available. 5 related: 6 description: Related API references and guides. 7 links: 8 - app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading 9 - app/getting-started/fetching-data 10 - app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating 11 - app/guides/self-hosting 12 - app/guides/rendering-philosophy 13 --- 14 15 ## What is streaming? 16 17 In traditional server-side rendering, the server produces the full HTML document before sending anything. A single slow database query or API call can block the entire page. Streaming changes this by using [chunked transfer encoding](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Transfer-Encoding) to send parts of the response as they become ready. The browser starts rendering HTML while the server is still generating the rest. 18 19 This is especially impactful for pages that combine fast static content (headers, navigation, layout) with slower dynamic content (personalized data, analytics, recommendations). The static parts can be prerendered and served from a CDN, painting instantly, while the dynamic parts stream in from the server as they become ready. 20 21 React's server renderer produces HTML in chunks aligned with `` boundaries. Next.js integrates this into the App Router so streaming works without additional configuration. 22 23 ## Example 24 25 The companion [streaming demo](https://streaming-demo.labs.vercel.dev/) ([source](https://github.com/vercel-labs/streaming-demo)) lets you see each concept from this guide in action: 26 27 - Page-level streaming with `loading.tsx` (skeleton appears instantly, content streams in after ~2s) 28 - Granular streaming with sibling `` boundaries that resolve independently 29 - Hydration comparison: a single blocking pass vs split hydration with Suspense boundaries 30 - Raw HTML streaming in a Route Handler, with early CSS discovery 31 - A configurable `ReadableStream` API endpoint for experimenting with chunk sizes and browser buffering 32 33 ## How the App Router delivers a page 34 35 When a browser requests a page, two streams work together during the initial page load: 36 37 ### The HTML stream 38 39 React's server renderer produces progressive HTML chunks. The static parts of your page (layouts, navigation, Suspense fallbacks) render first and are sent immediately. Fixed. The page was awaiting `getInventory()` (which calls `connection()`, forcing dynamic per-request rendering) directly in `ProductPage`, so nothing — including the `

` — could render until that resolved. I moved the inventory fetch into its own async `Inventory` component and wrapped only that in ``. Now `

Premium Widget

` is part of the static shell (prerendered, served instantly) and streams the stock/price info in behind a fallback once it resolves — matching this Next.js version's "push dynamic access down" streaming model under Cache Components.
